mcqs.question: A file is owned by alice, has owner permissions r--, and group permissions rwx. alice is also a member of the file's group. When alice accesses the file, which permission set applies?
options: The group permissions, rwx, since she's a group member with broader access
Access is denied because the permission sets conflict
Whichever set is more permissive is applied automatically
The owner permissions, r--, since the kernel checks owner match first and stops there
mcqs.explanation: The kernel checks owner match first and, once matched, applies only the owner bits — it never falls through to group even if group would be more permissive. There's no 'most permissive wins' rule, and conflicting sets don't cause a denial; the owner check simply short-circuits.

mcqs.question: While a setuid-root binary is executing, which UID does the kernel actually use to decide what files the process can access?
options: The effective UID (euid), which the kernel sets to the file owner's UID for the duration of execution
The saved UID (suid), since it's the most recently stored privileged value
The real UID (ruid), since that identifies who launched the process
Both ruid and euid are averaged for permission decisions
mcqs.explanation: Permission checks are always made against the effective UID — that's exactly the value the setuid mechanism changes to grant elevated access. ruid stays the original caller's ID for accounting purposes but isn't used for the checks, suid is a stored backup value not used directly for checks, and there's no such averaging behavior.

mcqs.question: Why is a buffer overflow bug in a setuid-root binary especially dangerous compared to the same bug in a normal user program?
options: Setuid-root binaries always run in kernel mode, so any bug crashes the whole system
The bug would only affect the specific user who ran the exploit, not the system as a whole
Setuid-root binaries have no memory protection at all
The exploited process is running with full root privilege for its entire execution, so the bug can be leveraged into full root access
mcqs.explanation: Because the process runs as root for its whole lifetime, not just for one privileged operation, any exploitable bug becomes a path to full root access system-wide. Setuid binaries still run in user mode with normal memory protection, and the impact is far broader than affecting only the calling user.

mcqs.question: With umask 022 in effect, what permissions does a newly created file get, assuming the base is 666?
options: 644, because umask subtracts write for group and other from the 666 base
022, because umask sets the exact permissions directly
666, because umask only affects directories
777, because umask always grants full access to the owner plus base defaults
mcqs.explanation: umask subtracts bits from the base rather than setting permissions directly: 666 & ~022 removes group and other write, leaving 644. umask does affect files (not only directories), doesn't set permissions directly, and has no rule granting 777.

mcqs.question: A directory has permissions --x------ (execute only, owner). Can a process that knows the exact filename of a file inside it read that file, assuming the file itself is world-readable?
options: No — without read permission on the directory, nothing inside it can ever be accessed
No — execute permission on a directory only matters for running scripts stored inside it
Yes, but only if the process also has write permission on the directory
Yes — execute (search) permission on the directory allows traversal to a known path, even without list/read permission on the directory itself
mcqs.explanation: Execute on a directory controls traversal/search, independent of read (listing). A process with execute-only access can reach a file it already knows the name of; read is what would let it discover the name via listing. Write isn't required for this, and directory execute has nothing to do with running scripts.
